title: torch.compile slower or failing for GNN training with dynamic NeighborLoader batches
body: I am benchmarking a simple GCN trained with NeighborLoader, where mini-batches have dynamic shapes. Simple gather/scatter compile tests pass for both static and dynamic shapes, but on this training benchmark eager mode is faster than torch.compile. The logs show torch._dynamo reaching its cache-size limit because tensor sizes and strides vary between batches. I am using a PyTorch 1.14.0a0 source build with CUDA 12.0 on Ubuntu 20.04 and NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and I linked the benchmark script and full logs.

symptoms_visible: My simple GCN uses NeighborLoader batches whose node and edge dimensions vary, and eager training is faster than torch.compile.
The compile logs repeatedly reach torch._dynamo's cache-size limit with size and stride mismatches between batches.
N0.label: N0 dynamic NeighborLoader regression reported

symptoms_visible: After building the suggested PyTorch branch, the compiled training run terminates with a segmentation fault.
N1_x.label: N1_x training branch segfault aftermath

symptoms_visible: The compiled training run on the branch still terminates with a segmentation fault.
N2.label: N2 old Triton backend identified

symptoms_visible: With the newer Triton source build and dynamic=True, compilation raises a size() TypeError because the dimension argument is a SymInt.
N2_x.label: N2_x newer Triton dynamic-shape error aftermath

symptoms_visible: After applying the suggested dynamic-shape configuration patch, the forward pass gets farther but backward compilation raises AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute '_has_symbolic_sizes_strides'.
N3_x.label: N3_x configuration hack aftermath

symptoms_visible: With the latest PyTorch, Triton, PyG and pyg-lib sources in April, Inductor completes training, but eager averages about 0.828 seconds per epoch while compiled training averages about 1.081 seconds.
The run warns that split reduction could not be used with dynamic shapes and performance may be worse.
N4_x.label: N4_x correctness restored but performance remains slower

symptoms_visible: On my updated PyG NeighborLoader training benchmark, torch.compile completes dynamic-batch training and is about 20% faster than eager mode.
N_terminal.label: terminal dynamic training works with measured speedup

solution.intent: Build the proposed training-support branch and retry the NeighborLoader workload with backward compilation.
solution.concrete_example: Build the linked PyTorch branch containing the training changes and rerun the complete epoch, including loss.backward().

edges.comment: Messages c2-c3, reporter's system: the maintainer asked whether this was training and suggested the linked branch. The reporter built it and the compiled model segfaulted, so that branch alone was not a resolution.

question_patterns: Which Triton backend and source revision is this container using?
Can you check whether the container has the older or newer Triton backend?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I was not initially sure how to check because I was just calling torch.compile in our February container. After checking with a colleague, I confirmed that the container was still using the old Triton backend, built from the Triton commit pinned by the PyTorch checkout.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I confirmed the crash occurs with a fresh build of the current Triton backend rather than the old pinned backend.
The container uses the old pinned Triton backend, but I built its wheel manually rather than installing a prebuilt wheel.

edges.comment: Messages c4-c6, reporter's system: the maintainer asked which Triton backend was present. The reporter first said they did not know, then confirmed that the February container used the old backend.

solution.intent: Replace the old pinned Triton backend with a current source build while keeping the training-support PyTorch branch, then retry dynamic compilation.
solution.concrete_example: Install a current Triton source build, rebuild the training-capable PyTorch branch, and rerun the model with torch.compile(..., dynamic=True).

edges.comment: Messages c6-c9, reporter's system: the reporter rebuilt with the suggested branch and newer Triton. After correcting the script to set dynamic=True, the run failed because size() received a SymInt dimension, so updating Triton did not by itself resolve dynamic training.

solution.intent: Temporarily change the dynamic-shape configuration so Python integer and float values are specialized, allowing the workload to pass the immediate SymInt size error.
solution.concrete_example: Patch enable_dynamic so dynamic_shapes and specialize_int_float are both enabled, then rebuild and rerun the full training workload.

edges.comment: Messages c10-c16, reporter's system: the maintainer explicitly called this a hack rather than the real fix. The reporter applied it with the training branch; backward compilation then failed on an integer symbolic placeholder.

solution.intent: Move off the temporary patches and retest with current PyTorch, Triton, PyG and pyg-lib sources containing the intervening dynamic-training correctness improvements.
solution.concrete_example: Rebuild the benchmark environment from the latest PyTorch, Triton, PyG and pyg-lib sources and rerun the same NeighborLoader training script.

edges.comment: Messages c24-c29 and c43, reporter's system: several compiler failures were fixed upstream. On the reporter's April latest-source environment, Inductor finally completed training, but the original performance complaint remained because compiled epochs were slower than eager.

solution.intent: Use a current compatible PyTorch, Triton and PyG stack for dynamic NeighborLoader training, measure warmed-up execution with correct CUDA synchronization, and set expectations that this overhead-bound workload may receive a modest speedup rather than the previously reported twofold gain.
solution.concrete_example: Retest the original NeighborLoader script on current source builds with torch.compile(..., dynamic=True), warm up compilation, and synchronize CUDA consistently around the measured regions. The reporter's subsequent run completed and measured roughly a 20% improvement over eager.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers derived the diagnosis across c23-c30 and c53-c54: the sequence of None inputs, symbolic placeholders, insufficient guards, overspecialization and dynamic split-reduction limitations reflected incomplete dynamic-shape training support. They also found graph breaks and CPU-side overhead, and determined that an extra CUDA synchronization between forward and backward inflated an earlier reported speedup. The reporter supplied raw tracebacks and timings, not those conclusions.

edges.comment: Messages c43-c57, reporter's system plus maintainer analysis: the April stack ran but was slower. Maintainers investigated synchronization and overhead in separate benchmark runs. In c57 the reporter retested the original PyG NeighborLoader script and personally reported a 20% torch.compile speedup, providing affected-user verification.

solution.intent: Move directly to a current compatible PyTorch, Triton and PyG stack, use dynamic compilation for the NeighborLoader workload, and benchmark warmed-up execution with consistent CUDA synchronization before deciding whether compilation improves performance.
solution.concrete_example: Update the compiler and PyG stack, run torch.compile(..., dynamic=True) on the original training script, warm up first, and synchronize CUDA consistently. Verify the result on the changing NeighborLoader batches rather than assuming the static microbenchmark's speedup will transfer.
solution.inference_hint: This shortcut represents proposing the eventual practical resolution immediately. The detailed symbolic-shape failures, upstream intermediate fixes, graph-break analysis and synchronization discrepancy were only established later in the thread.

edges.comment: Shortcut from the opening state so an agent that immediately recommends the eventual current-stack and sound-benchmarking resolution can match without being forced through the branch, Triton and configuration attempts that failed on the reporter's system.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted technical picture: the crashes and recompilations came from incomplete dynamic-shape training support across Dynamo/AOTAutograd/Inductor, while the remaining GNN performance was constrained by graph breaks, dynamic reduction limitations and CPU-side overhead.

Must ground the diagnosis in the collected evidence: varying-size cache-limit warnings, the SymInt size failure, the backward symbolic-placeholder failure, and the later run that completed but remained slower.

Must recommend testing with a current compatible PyTorch, Triton and PyG stack on the original dynamic NeighborLoader training workload, rather than treating the old training branch, a Triton-only update, or the integer-specialization hack as the complete fix.

Must not promise the roughly twofold gain from the separate basic-GNN benchmark; CUDA synchronization placement affected that comparison, and the reporter ultimately measured a more modest approximately 20% speedup.

Must ask the reporter to verify correctness and performance on the original changing-batch training benchmark before declaring resolution; the case is resolved only after the reporter's own updated run completes and shows a speedup.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced ML infrastructure user who builds PyTorch, Triton and PyG from source in CUDA containers, edits benchmark scripts, applies patches, and can provide full Python tracebacks and timing results.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, concise and collaborative; posts raw commands, logs and measurements, corrects earlier misunderstandings, asks directly for fixes and timeline expectations, and repeatedly retests on updated source builds.
